messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Javier Moreno, a 54-year-old Latino business owner, came to treatment after months of telling himself he should be able to handle this on his own. Before he returned to the United States, he had spent time as a relief worker in a war zone, helping move food and medical supplies through neighborhoods where civilians crowded close to the trucks and gunfire could break out without warning. What stayed with him most was not one single image but the press of bodies around him when distributions began, the way grateful faces could turn panicked in an instant, and the crack of gunshots that cut through moments that were supposed to feel hopeful. He remembered one afternoon especially clearly: children had been laughing near a supply line, adults were reaching toward him, and he had felt a brief rush of relief that this delivery might go smoothly. Then shots rang out nearby, people surged toward him, and that small feeling of safety vanished so fast that he now mistrusted it.

Back home, Javier resumed running his business, trying to move through long workdays as if he had simply returned from a difficult assignment. Instead, ordinary moments began to carry the shape of the war zone. If a customer or employee stepped too close while speaking to him in the office, his body tightened before he could think. Loud popping sounds from the street, a car backfiring, even something that resembled gunfire in the distance could make his attention snap outward. What unsettled him in a more confusing way were moments that should have felt good. A relaxed dinner with his wife, laughter with a friend, or even a brief sense of pride when the business had a strong day could abruptly feel dangerous to him, as though feeling good meant he was about to be blindsided again. Because of that, he had begun to meet even pleasant moments with suspicion.

As these reactions took hold, Javier developed ways of managing them that made sense to him in the moment. He started carrying a weapon, telling himself he was being practical, that a man who had seen how quickly things turned could not afford to be unprepared. At work he positioned himself carefully and paid attention to who came near him. When a trigger hit, especially a loud sound or someone entering his space too fast, he would later go over and over why the event had happened to him at all—why he had been there, why he had survived, what he should have understood sooner. He could spend hours mentally circling the same questions without getting any closer to an answer. At other times, when the unease built and he sensed one of those falsely “good” moments beginning, he found himself picking arguments with employees, with vendors, and eventually with his wife. Creating conflict gave him somewhere to put the tension. Anger felt more usable than vulnerability.

Over the following months, those habits began feeding the very sensitivity he was trying to control. Carrying a weapon kept Javier oriented toward danger in every setting; in his store, a customer leaning in to ask a question could feel like a threat simply because he was already braced to defend himself. The arguments he provoked also left him more keyed up, so that afterward he noticed closeness, noise, and even warmth from other people as if they were warnings. His rumination worked similarly. The more he revisited the event, trying to force meaning from it, the more alive its atmosphere seemed in the present. Gunshot-like sounds felt less like reminders and more like immediate alarms. Even positive emotions became harder to tolerate, because he had trained himself to search every calm moment for what might shatter it.

This cycle began to alter his life in concrete ways. Employees had started commenting on how quickly he became confrontational, and one long-term staff member had asked to work fewer hours with him. At home, his wife no longer knew when a pleasant evening might turn into an argument Javier himself seemed unable to explain. He hated that part most: he could see that he was spoiling the very moments he wanted back, yet when things felt light or close or safe, he was certain something bad was about to follow. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted from staying armed, from scanning other people’s distance from him, and from replaying the same questions in his head. He came in frightened by how much of his life had narrowed around these reactions, and quietly hopeful that he might learn how to be near people, hear ordinary sounds, and feel a good moment without immediately preparing for disaster.
